thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why should prices be stored in integer cents (e.g. 1999 for $19.99) rather than double?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: Floating-point numbers (double/float) cannot represent decimal fractions like 0.1 exactly due to binary IEEE 754 representation, leading to rounding errors (e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004). Storing integer cents guarantees exact financial arithmetic.

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: How does LinkedHashSet preserve chronological browsing history when an item is viewed a second time?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: If an item is already present in a LinkedHashSet, calling add() does nothing and does NOT change its position. To refresh recency, you must first call remove(item) and then add(item), moving it to the end of the iteration order!

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why use Map.merge() over containsKey() + put() for cart aggregation?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: Map.merge(key, qty, Integer::sum) performs the lookup, null check, and addition in a single hash operation, making code cleaner and twice as fast as separate contains/get/put calls.

hintSystem.level2Implementation: Pass productId, quantity to add, and Integer::sum as the remapping function.

hintSystem.level1Conceptual: LinkedHashSet only updates insertion order for new elements. To update an existing element, delete it first.

activities.title: Practical Context: Supermarket Tally Sheet & Display Aisle
activities.description: How retail systems combine fast tallying, recency memory, and multi-tier categorization.
activities.content:
Imagine shopping in a modern supermarket. In the grocery aisle, products are arranged on shelves categorized by price, brand rating, and specials (Catalog Comparator sorting).

As you place items into your shopping cart, you don't keep 5 separate cartons of milk scattered in random corners; you tally 'Milk x 5' on a clip-board (Map quantity aggregation). If you reconsider and pick an item you viewed earlier, you move it to the front of your cart (LinkedHashSet recency).

At the checkout counter, the cashier scans the tally sheet, confirms the warehouse has all items in stock, prints an itemized receipt, and deducts the inventory in a single atomic transaction. Java Collections model this exact flow.

activities.title: Architecture of E-Commerce Cart & Catalog Engine
activities.description: Technical analysis of Map aggregation, LinkedHashSet ordering, and fluent Comparator sorting.
activities.content:
### Formal Computer Science Definition
An e-commerce retail engine is a composite state machine coordinating an associative tally map (`Map<ID, Integer>`), a recency-ordered doubly-linked set (`LinkedHashSet<T>`), and an orderable catalog projection sorted via multi-tiered total preorder relations (`Comparator<T>`).

### Architectural Map & Data Flow

```
                                ECommerceStoreEngine
                                         |
     +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
     |                                   |                                   |
Catalog (List<Product>)         ShoppingCart (Map<ID, Integer>)     BrowsingHistory (LinkedHashSet)
- Multi-criteria Comparators    - O(1) Map.merge(id, qty, sum)      - Insertion-ordered set
- Price / Rating / Name         - Validates stock before addition   - remove(p) + add(p) refreshes recency
     |                                   |
     +-----------------------------------+ 
                                         |
                                [Checkout Event]
                                1. Verify all quantities <= stock
                                2. Deduct stock atomically
                                3. Emit immutable OrderReceipt
```

### Key Implementation Rules
1. **Integer Cent Financials**: Never use `double` or `float` for prices. Always store prices in integer cents (`long priceCents = 1999L`).
2. **`Map.merge` Idiom**: `cart.merge(id, qty, Integer::sum)` combines null checks, key creation, and arithmetic in one hash probe.
3. **`LinkedHashSet` Recency**: Calling `add()` on an existing element is a no-op! You must `remove(item)` first, then `add(item)` to relocate it to the MRU position.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using cart.merge(id, qty, Integer::sum) over cart.put(id, cart.getOrDefault(id, 0) + qty)?
options: It serializes the cart over JSON automatically
It performs the lookup, null check, and accumulation in a single hash probe, improving performance and readability
It prevents concurrent thread modifications without locking
questions.explanation: Map.merge executes in a single bucket lookup rather than two separate operations (get and put), minimizing hash table probes and eliminating boilerplate.

questions.question: Why is LinkedHashSet used for browsing history instead of standard HashSet or ArrayList?
options: LinkedHashSet prevents duplicates (unlike ArrayList) while preserving insertion/recency order (unlike HashSet)
LinkedHashSet uses less memory than HashSet
questions.explanation: HashSet has no ordering guarantees; ArrayList allows duplicate entries. LinkedHashSet combines hash lookup for duplicate prevention with a doubly-linked list for chronological ordering.

questions.question: Why should prices always be modeled as integer cents (e.g., long priceCents) instead of double in retail engines?
options: long integers execute faster on 32-bit CPUs
Floating-point numbers produce binary rounding errors (e.g., 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3) that lead to financial discrepancies
The Java Collections Framework does not support double in Maps
questions.explanation: IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic introduces rounding drift in base-10 financial operations. Storing currency in integer cents ensures exact arithmetic.

activities.title: Principal Architect Retail System Design Interview Questions
activities.description: Staff-level design problems on cart concurrency, flash sale inventory, and database synchronization.

questions.question: How do you prevent inventory overselling when 5,000 customers try to purchase the last 10 units of an item simultaneously?
questions.answer:
To prevent overselling:
1. Use an atomic counter (AtomicInteger or Redis DECR / SQL 'UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1') at reservation time rather than checkout completion time.
2. When adding to cart, grant a temporary reservation holding the stock for a bounded window (e.g. 10 minutes).
3. If checkout is completed within the window, the reservation transitions to committed; if the TTL expires, the stock is automatically returned to the inventory pool.

questions.question: How do you design a scalable shopping cart that survives application server restarts without querying the database on every item add?
questions.answer:
1. Store active cart state in a distributed in-memory cache (Redis Hash: HINCRBY cart:userId productId qty).
2. Read and modify the cart in Redis with sub-millisecond latency.
3. Emit an asynchronous event to a message queue (Kafka) to persist cart state to PostgreSQL lazily.
4. If the app server crashes, the user's cart is instantly retrieved from Redis upon reconnect.
